Bayanda Walaza - The World's Fastest Teenager

By: Julian Sun | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Meet the world's fastest teenager: South African sprint sensation Bayanda Walaza

Unique Selling Point:
An intimate portrait of one of South Africa's rising superstars: 18-year-old Bayanda Walaza.

With the world at his feet, we provide a compelling journey that takes in his past, present and potential future

From his compelling backstory of a young boy who at just 8 years old, dreamt of emulating his heroine Caster Semenya in winning Olympic Gold to his current status as Olympic Silver medalist and 100m, 200m winner at the world junior champs, could he become the next Usain Bolt?


Summary:
He has an amazing back story:

He comes from Katlehong

at 8 years old, he wrote a letter to his heroine: Caster Semenya, saying he wanted to emulate her feats of winning Olympic gold

His mother Tholiwe was also a sprinter in her youth and he’s inherited her sprinting genes

She’s raised him as a single mother, after his dad was murdered when Bayanda was just 10

Since he burst onto the scene, he’s had offers from colleges in the USA to go attend on an athletics scholarship but he’s decided to stay in SA and continue to work with his current coach Thabo Matebedi

“I’m not going to change coaches because that can cause a lot of difficulties. It’s better to chill with the coach that’s working for me. He made me get two gold medals, and silver at the Olympics, so why must I leave him?

Press Release:


World’s Fastest Teen
When he was eight years old, Bayanda Walaza wrote a letter to his hero, Caster Semenya. But it wasn’t just fan mail: it was a message to his future self, the athlete that he dreamed of becoming. And a decade later, Bayanda rocketed to stardom. The first South African to win an Olympic medal while still in high school, he’s stacking up international medals and national records – and at just 19, he's nowhere near his limit. We meet the sprinting prodigy with the world at his feet.

Script:


Bayanda Walaza Script

Mac V/O: The 100m sprint, the crown jewel of track and field…Over time, it has produced some of the greatest athletes ever. From Jesse Owens defying Nazi ideology, to the blistering power of world-record holder Usain Bolt. Only 190 men have breached the 10-second barrier… The man who holds the world record is also “the fastest human alive.”

Mac: The 100m sprint is the most watched event at the Olympic Games for a reason, for it is the ultimate test of pure speed. Names like Carl Lewis and Usain Bolt have etched their names in history with their raw pace. Now comes another daring to step into the footsteps of these giants. His name is Bayanda Walaza

Mac: In August last year, this 19-year-old sprint sensation made history as the first South African to win an Olympic medal while still in high school, as part of the men's 4x100m relay team along with Shaun Maswanganyi, Bradley Nkoana, and anchor Akani Simbine at the Paris Games.

Bayanda: We see Akani coming from the back, catching up. So we’re kinda scared, looks like you might win this, we might win this… get there… silver medal! Oh it feels it felt like the world just paused a minute, it paused, you know like is this for real? And from there, then my life started changing!

Mac: With an Olympic Silver medal under his belt, just a few weeks later, Bayanda Walaza took centre stage at the World Junior Championships in Peru, storming to gold in both the 100 and 200m races, earning the moniker: The fastest teenager in the world.

Bayanda: I truly appreciate the World Juniors more because of that was about me, you know?

Mac: It’s something that you did for yourself?

Bayanda: Yes, I did for myself. And it's something that gave me that name of the fastest teenager in the whole world.

Mac: His rise to fame is the culmination of a dream inspired by South African gold-medal athlete Caster Semenya

Mac: When you were a little boy, you wrote a letter to Caster Semenya. Tell me a little bit about that.

Bayanda: it wasn't a letter to Caster Semenya, but it was like planning for what I want to do in future, you know, because as I was watching Caster Semenya races, she was always winning and all of that. So I wrote a letter saying that, you know, when I grow up, I want to be like her, get all the money, buy my mom a house and live the life that she's living. You know, it was like a kind of a letter to myself telling me that this is the the future that I must reach.

Mac: It’s a future that seemed out of reach when, as a child, he witnessed his father gunned down.

Bayanda: It was something else, you know, it was tragic. It took my it took me out. You know, there was a point where I almost even quit school. At some point when I think about it, makes me strong, you know, to be like, bra, you overcome this, you know? Before I run, as I pray, when it’s serious races I also call upon my father. I tell him, bra,

Mac: I'm here now.

Bayanda: I’m here Baba, take me to the finish line!

Mac: For the past 3 years, Bayanda has been trained by Thabo Matebedi. More than a coach, he’s also become a father figure.

Thabo: Bayanda grew up with some challenges at home where the father passed on, that’s what actually led to take Bayanda in my group. I can still remember telling his mom that I feel goosebumps, this boy’s going to be fast!

Upsound: Thabo: Nothing will surprise you in life, a life without surprises is boring!

Mac: Coach Thabo Matebadi speaks about you like a son. How is your relationship with him and why have you stuck with him?

Bayanda: It was a kind of a roller coaster start.He kept on asking me, what do you want? It was hard. We were fighting most of the time till a point where it came to ease. But it started being easy when I started being talking to him about opening my heart to him, telling him what do I want.

Mac: It wasn’t long before he saw improvements on the track

Bayanda: I started being fast. You know, I went there, I was a 10.5 guy. I went, I said, 10.3 ok we still like okay progression. And then I went to 10.1 and then we were like, nah, man, this is the coach that I need to stay

Mac: This is my guy

Bayanda: The improvement is here!

Mac: It’s easy to forget that Bayanda’s body is still developing. His physical conditioning is managed through a special gym programme designed by strength and conditioning coach Karen Gibbs

Karen: So with Bayanda, I'm very happy we managed to start when he was quite young, as we are able to manage his transition from junior athlete to a senior athlete, because that’s where we lose the majority of these talented sprinters.

Upsound Karen: Breathe out, Breathe out and back

Mac: But while she works on his physical conditioning, it’s his mental strength that sets him apart.

Karen Gibbs: I would say anything that makes Bayanda special, in my view, at least at the moment, is not his running style. It is the ability to, to elevate his performance when it really matters. When the pressure is on, he has an ability to almost calm the nerves and we can see if we know. Well enough by now to know when Bayanda is switched on. And that's not something you can teach, an athlete either has that or they don't.

Mac: The 100m is over in under 10 seconds, but what goes through the mind on a sprinter from the starting blocks to the finish line?

Mac: As you’re going down, getting your fingers into the lane, what’s happening in your mind now?

Bayanda: That’s when you start shaking, you can feel that adrenaline coming in and now you’re going, you know?

Bayanda: The start it’s all about drive you know, it’s all the power, it’s all the focus, being low, as low as possible, you know

Bayanda: Also running is about momentum, so as you boom boom, you cannot start already drrrrruuum really fast. So as from there it’s like you’re building up on it, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom. So yeah at the first 10m it’s still early to be up from the drive but it’s a place where you have to start showing that you’re now transitioning to becoming tall.

Mac: So is it high knees but also trying to kick forward…

Bayanda: It’s like a stride yes! It’s like a kigh knee, stride in some kind of a way

Mac: You’re almost galloping like a horse

Bayanda: It’s like you’re pushing yourself to the front. So that’s where the race starts to be fun, that’s where you see people in the stands

Mac: Now you’re seeing your fans, hearing the noise

Bayanda: But in the race you don’t even hear them, I won’t lie. You won’t hear anything now because now you’re zoned in yeah!

Mac: Since he burst onto the world stage, Bayanda has made headlines, not just for his blistering speed, but for a very unorthodox running style. His form is like a "galloping horse" or even a "windmill" when at full stride, earning him the nickname "Wobble Wobble.

Thabo: It’s not a running style, it’s his survival mode. If you look at Bayanda at 60%, run 80%, he has a normal way of running. But once he’s under pressure, he tries to survive. So he’s fighting back to win the race. So it’s not actually a style, you can’t change and if you change that, you’re gonna destroy the boy

Bayanda: The last 30 or last 40, that’s where my kick. That thing happens automatically even though I go hard, I’m like, I’m not moving. Let me go even harder, that’s why I think also, that’s there’s also that movement because this person is trying to push till the finish.

Mac: We can see it, you can actually see it in your videos that there’s a change, almost like with your arms, you’re pushing

Bayanda: And what coach sees in that is that he said that is my survival instinct.

Mac: Wow!

Mac: Bayanda has continued to excel on the track in 2025, breaking the magical 10-second barrier last month. He stands on the cusp of greatness, hoping to be the first South African to write the next chapter in the storied history of the 100m sprint.

Mac: So the world record is 9.58, right. Bayanda ran a 9.99. What's it going to take to break that to what is it a fourth of a second or what is it

Thabo: It's going to take another three years to get there. This is just 36 months is like a cellphone contract. Okay. So it sounds it does. It sounds long when you say three years, but he's going to take us another three years to to get to that level. And I think he has the ability to do it.

Mac: How would you describe Bayanda is a word?

Thabo: Bayanda the great!

Bayanda: I believe that I'm going to be something great. I believe that the. Well, you know who Walaza is. You know, that's the dream. I also want to pursue. I want everywhere I go, people know that this guy made a change, especially in South Africa. You know, there was change because of this guy. So I believe that I'm going to I believe that I'm going to be I'm going to be great

Mac: and we’re a 100% behind you.


PROMOS

Promo 1:
Bayanda Walaza burst onto the world stage last year when he won Olympic Silver in the mens 4x100m relay in Paris.

Bayanda: Ah from there, my life started changing

Can this new sprint sensation cope with the pressure of being dubbed the fastest teenager in the world?

Bayanda: The whole world will know who Walaza is!


Promo 2:
He’s been dubbed the fastest teenager in the world and broke the 10-second barrier just weeks ago.

Is 19-year-old Bayanda Walaza the next big thing in world athletics?
